summary: SHFD (The Single Harmonized Flame Detector) joins 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections over Brazil, from 2001 to 2026, into one record. The older MODIS satellites and the newer VIIRS see the same fires differently. VIIRS has sharper pixels and counts about four times more hot spots, so the raw record jumps in 2012 even though the fires did not. We used the ten years when both flew together, 2012 to 2021, to learn how their counts relate in each region and month, and converted the older years to the VIIRS scale. Tested on years the method never saw, the national yearly error is 1.6%. On top of this record we built a free web app. Anyone can draw an area or type a place and see every hot spot in it, its fire season, its worst years and whether this month is above or below a usual year. Fire managers, researchers and citizens need this to compare today with the past. On one scale, 2001 to 2011 averaged 1.73 million hot spots a year, against 1.22 million in 2012 to 2025.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

SHFD (The Single Harmonized Flame Detector) puts 25 years of NASA fire detections over Brazil, from 2001 to 2026, on one scale. NASA has watched these fires with two generations of satellites. MODIS has flown since 2001 with pixels of about 1 km. VIIRS joined in 2012 with 375 m pixels, sees small fires that MODIS misses and counts about four times more hot spots. Put the two side by side and the record jumps in 2012, even though the fires did not.

We fixed this in three steps. First we removed weak detections and fixed heat sources such as gas flares and factories. Then we used 2012 to 2021, when both satellites flew together, to measure how many more hot spots VIIRS records than MODIS in each region and calendar month, separately for Terra and Aqua and refined in areas of about 200 km. Last, we applied that factor to every MODIS hot spot from 2001 to 2011, so the older years now sit on the VIIRS scale.

To test it, we hid each year from 2012 to 2021, rebuilt the factors without it and predicted it. For all of Brazil the yearly error averaged 1.6% and the monthly correlation was 0.998. In areas of about 200 km, 92% of years and 66% of months landed within 20% of what VIIRS saw. Two identical VIIRS satellites agree in 85% of months, so that is about the best any conversion can reach.

On top of this record we built a free web app. You draw an area on the map, or type a latitude, longitude and distance, and the app lists every hot spot in it as a table or CSV. It also shows when the local fire season starts, the best months to prepare, a fire calendar with every month of every year, and whether this month is above or below a usual year.

What benefits does it have?

Anyone can compare this year with any year since 2001, without the false jump in 2012. The app uses plain English and simple charts, so nobody needs to know which satellite saw what. There are no fixed regions: you pick the area. The code, the processed data, 26 automated tests and the validation are public on GitHub.

What is the intended impact?

We built it for firefighters, fire managers, farmers, city officials, researchers and anyone who lives near fire. They can see where and when fires happen, find their local fire season and get ready earlier. The harmonized record also corrects a wrong reading of the past. The raw data suggest fire grew after 2012. On one scale, 2001 to 2011 averaged 1.73 million hot spots a year against 1.22 million in 2012 to 2025, and September 2005 had 683,818 hot spots while September 2024 had 598,825. MODIS is being retired and VIIRS S-NPP has sent no data since 2 November 2026, so the method also lets this record continue on the next satellites. Next we want to cover the whole world and move the monthly agreement from 66% closer to 85%.

What tools did you use?

Python with pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, Apache Parquet, Shapely, Matplotlib and Jupyter. Streamlit, Plotly and Folium/Leaflet for the app, with Esri imagery as the base map, hosted free on Streamlit Community Cloud. Git and GitHub for version control and tests. Two personal laptops.

How is the project creative?

NASA FIRMS shows each satellite as its own layer. We gave every old hot spot its own weight on the new scale. Because of that, any area and any period, down to a single day, adds up on the same scale, and the map, the totals and the calendar all share it. You can put September 2005 next to September 2024 and read them the same way.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty came first. Every number was tested on years the method never saw, and we report what failed: day/night factors, neighbourhood smoothing, power-law and quantile-mapping conversions all did worse and were dropped. We also state the limits. A hot spot marks heat, not the size of a fire. Clouds hide fires. Days with no satellite data stay empty in the charts, so a gap reads as missing data. Small areas and single days are less precise than large areas and whole months. For non-experts we kept satellite names out of the app and show only the joined record. Any area over 25 years loads in about a second, and everything we used is free and open.
